body:
Let me see if I understand the two sides of the debate here.

Per my reading of the current specification, inserting a link element (whether cloned or not) should synchronously start the fetching process. However, because fetching always goes in parallel and then queues a task to complete, this means that the actual application of the styles should be async. "Application of the styles" can be measured by:

- Whether `linkElement.sheet` exists
- Whether `getComputedStyle()` returns the updated styles from the sheet, or not.

Your claim is that in Firefox and Safari, cloning a `<link>` and then inserting it results in the styles being applied synchronously, not asynchronously. Is that correct? Or is it just that they render before the next animation frame, i.e. within 16 milliseconds?

Can you say more about the Safari and Firefox behavior in general? E.g., is `clonedLinkElement.sheet === originalLinkElement.sheet`? Or is it some sort of deep copy?

In general we try to minimize the number of cloning steps on the web platform, as every one of them adds implicit magic which is hard to predict. So I don't think we necessarily want to undertake a larger project of generalizing this to all sorts of resources. But converging the spec to match 2/3 browser behavior is generally reasonable.

> Your claim is that in Firefox and Safari, cloning a <link> and then inserting it results in the styles being applied synchronously, not asynchronously. Is that correct? Or is it just that they render before the next animation frame, i.e. within 16 milliseconds?

```
                const cloned_link = link.cloneNode();
                alert(cloned_link.sheet);              // Null everywhere, as per spec
                shadow.appendChild(cloned_link);
                alert("Clone element sheet: " + cloned_link.sheet); // Available immediately in Firefox + Safari, null in Chrome (until you requestAnimationFrame)
                alert("Sheets equal? " + (cloned_link.sheet == link.sheet)); // False everywhere, so it's a deep clone (as expected)
```

The `alert` blocks paint while it's open. My understanding that the value being available at that point indicates it's synchronous (vs happening before the next render frame). Is that correct? I also tried inserting thousands of elements in Firefox at the same time (which would take longer than a frame to paint), and it's still returning the value for `cloned_link.sheet` immediately, before anything is painted.

> In general we try to minimize the number of cloning steps on the web platform, as every one of them adds implicit magic which is hard to predict. So I don't think we necessarily want to undertake a larger project of generalizing this to all sorts of resources. But converging the spec to match 2/3 browser behavior is generally reasonable.

This makes sense, given how many elements we don't want to special case. But I'm wondering if some sort of generic phrase here could cover all of the elements with underlying resources like this. 

However, Hoch pointed out the https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#the-input-element has specific steps for cloning: "The [cloning steps](https://dom.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-node-clone-ext) for [input](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#the-input-element) elements given node, copy, and subtree are to propagate the [value](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#concept-fe-value), [dirty value flag](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#concept-fe-dirty), [checkedness](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#concept-fe-checked), and [dirty checkedness flag](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/input.html#concept-input-checked-dirty-flag) from node to copy."

Looks like `textarea`, `script`, `input`, and `template` have special cases. But none of these appear to mention what do to with underlying resources, so maybe we can get away with a generic statement such as, "if the element has an underlying resource, the user agent may optimize copying that resource as long as it is not made available until a fetch for that resource would have been initiated." or something along those lines.

If it's non-null immediately after the `appendChild()` call it's indeed not per the specification.

cc @emilio @noamr @rniwa

> If it's non-null immediately after the `appendChild()` call it's indeed not per the specification.
> 
> cc [@emilio](https://github.com/emilio) [@noamr](https://github.com/noamr) [@rniwa](https://github.com/rniwa)

I would argue that being available immediately is what web developers want in this case, as it avoids a FOUC. If Chromium is the only browser per-spec but has an FOUC every time, I think we should update the spec and fix Chromium.

I already have a fix for Chromium in review and am happy to update the spec's language here.
Maybe? Did you test it across different origin documents or documents in different tabs?

> Maybe? Did you test it across different origin documents or documents in different tabs?

Good questions, I will look into this and report here. By "different tabs", you mean via another window via `window.open`? Because otherwise we can't call `cloneNode` on an element in another tab, right?

Also interesting to note, Chromium *is* synchronous in this case when the `<link>`'s  `href` is a dataURI (this is an optimization in the fetch steps). The repro zip in the bug demonstrates this: https://issues.chromium.org/issues/396174245

Note that the `load` event still fires async in this case.

But yeah this in-memory cache of loaded stylesheets has been there in some shape or form since 1999 (mLoadedSheets in https://github.com/mozilla/gecko-dev/commit/0b7d088e69924969164d0ccd22cf8fcd77f9cca9).

@annevk - Firefox is also synchronous with cross-window cloning via `window.open`, which makes sense based on @emilio's comment above.

We can't clone nodes from cross-origin iframes and insert them into the main document, so I don't think this scenario is relevant.
Yeah, I made the cache work across documents in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1599160
OK so sounds like this is another case of https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6110

It sounds like we've converged on this being a memory cache issue, which is good. (Or at least, it reduces the number of special things in the system...)

In terms of impact on Chromium and unblocking your work there, my advice would be to proceed with making it synchronous, to match the other 2/3 browsers. It would be great if we could fix #6110 one day, but we shouldn't block interop on it.

Some other comments to clear up misconceptions:

> Looks like `textarea`, `script`, `input`, and `template` have special cases. But none of these appear to mention what do to with underlying resources, so maybe we can get away with a generic statement such as, "if the element has an underlying resource, the user agent may optimize copying that resource as long as it is not made available until a fetch for that resource would have been initiated." or something along those lines.

No, we can't have vague specification language like that. And as mentioned above, we want to minimize the number of cloning steps. So if we needed to add them, we'd do them one by one, with precise details for what "underlying resource" means. (E.g., the `sheet` property for style sheets.)

But thankfully in this case there's no cloning steps needed at all, just a memory cache!

> I would argue that being available immediately is what web developers want in this case, as it avoids a FOUC. If Chromium is the only browser per-spec but has an FOUC every time, I think we should update the spec and fix Chromium.

Be careful not to conflate synchronous with avoiding FOUC. You can avoid FOUC by applying styles any time within the next 16 ms. You don't need to apply synchronously.

So it's still possible to follow basically the current spec, and avoid FOUC. Chromium would just need to be faster about applying the styles from the memory cache, so that the posted task which applies the styles arrives before the next animation frame.

However, it sounds like Firefox and Safari's memory cache applies synchronously. It's not just "the fetch completes really fast"; it's "the fetch completes synchronously, without ever going in parallel + posting a task". That has implications for how we'd specify the memory cache, in #6110.

> We can't clone nodes from cross-origin iframes and insert them into the main document, so I don't think this scenario is relevant.

Pretty sure you can with `document.domain`.

It turns out the Chromium issue only happens with local files, due to a proprietary behavior to always do a full fetch for local files. This means this isn't an issue with the spec or a general interoperability issue, so I'll close it out.

I do think there may be room for an optimized clone algorithm that doesn't refetch nodes with resources, but that's tangential to this issue.
I'm not sure why you closed this. There's definitely still a difference between implementations and the specification.
There is, but we can roll it into #6110, right?
That seems fine, but we might want to retitle that issue then. And in that case we shouldn't close this as completed, but as a duplicate.

I mean, I'm not sure what we would retitle it as. We determined after eventual root-cause analysis that this is just a special case of the memory cache, and has nothing to do with cloning.

So I'll close this as duplicate.
Well, but this is clearly a different case from images.
Right, #6110 is about how the memory cache is much larger than the spec's existing "list of available images".

> Yeah, I made the cache work across documents in https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1599160

@emilio - I see that Firefox doesn't re-fetch when requested from a server with `Cache-Control: no-store`. Presumably that's due to the in-memory cache you referenced. Chrome will re-fetch (and hit this async behavior) with `Cache-Control: no-store`, which is what I would expect. This seems like a Firefox bug.

> I'm not sure why you closed this. There's definitely still a difference between implementations and the specification.

I'm still new to the protocols here, but that's good to know, thank you! I figured implementation-specific bugs should be tracked in their own bug databases, but I can see the value in tracking them here too in case the specs need to be updated.

I'm fine tracking this one as a case of #6110, as it doesn't really have anything to do with `cloneNode` as I had initially suspected.

Chrome will re-fetch (and hit this async behavior) with `Cache-Control: no-store`, which is what I would expect. This seems like a Firefox bug.

You mean within the same document or different documents? If the same document has loaded a resource we always reuse it, much like images. I took a look at the source and we do look at in-store but maybe there's a bug if you see it across documents.
I was referring to same-document. The potential bug is that `Cache-Control: no-store` is ignored with the in-memory cache behavior you described.

> I figured implementation-specific bugs should be tracked in their own bug databases

It's not an implementation-specific bug if the _specification_ doesn't describe what any implementation does and implementations are unlikely to change on this.

Yeah I agree this should not be closed, or at least a separate issue should be open to sort this out.

FWIW the same-document behavior not honoring no-cache / no-store is expected as of right now (and has been the behavior in Firefox since ~forever). I think images do something similar too.
